# The Archive of Bees

Honey never spoils. Jars of it have been pulled from Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and by all accounts were still edible—still golden, still sweet, still honey. The chemistry is almost aggressive about it: bees fan the nectar until nearly all the water has evaporated, and they add enzymes that make it acidic and faintly antiseptic. Microbes cannot get a footing. It is a food that refuses time.

But the chemistry is not the strange part. The strange part is the intimacy. Whoever sealed that tomb jar expected, at most, to feed the dead. Instead they left behind a taste. Open it after three thousand years and nothing has decayed, nothing needs interpretation, nothing is a ruin. Sweetness is one of the only things that can cross that distance intact.

Almost nothing else does. The literature of antiquity that we call a canon is, more honestly, a wreckage. Sophocles wrote well over a hundred plays; seven survive. Aeschylus wrote perhaps eighty; seven. Sappho's poems were once arranged in nine books; today we have one poem intact and a rubble of fragments, many preserved only because a grammarian quoted a couple of lines to illustrate a point of dialect. Some of the most admired poetry ever written persists in other people's footnotes. The classics are not so much a library as the surviving debris of a library, and the survival was arbitrary. It had almost nothing to do with merit.

Beowulf comes down to us in a single manuscript. One. It sat in a private library that caught fire in 1731, and you can still see the scorch creeping in from the edges; the fire got the margins, not the middle, and so we have the poem. Luck, not judgment. Archimedes' most daring work—the one where he handles infinities like a juggler—survived because a medieval monk scraped the ink off the parchment and wrote a book of prayers over it. The prayers were why the pages were kept. Beneath them, faint as a watermark, the geometry waited a thousand years. It took until 1906 for anyone to notice. That is the joke of the palimpsest: the destruction was the preservation. If the monk had simply thrown the old pages out, the geometry would have gone with them.

And then there is Lucretius, whose poem *On the Nature of Things* argues that everything is atoms moving through void, that the gods are indifferent to us, and that there is nothing in death to fear. It was written in the first century BC and copied for a thousand years afterward mostly by scribes who believed none of it, hanging by threads of parchment in monasteries. In 1417 a book hunter named Poggio pulled a copy from a shelf in a German monastery and carried it back to Italy, where it helped reseed the imagination of a whole civilization. Every work we still read is a survivor—of fires, worms, damp walls, ordinary indifference. For each one, imagine the hundred that met the damp wall.

We tell ourselves our own era will be different: everything digital, everything backed up, everything forever. This is almost exactly backwards. Paper and vellum are inert. A book just sits there, waiting, asking nothing. A digital file exists only while some machine agrees to interpret it, and the machines die young. In 1086 the Domesday Book recorded England in ink; you can still read it. In 1986 the BBC marked the anniversary with a new Domesday—a million volunteers, photographs and text, stored on laser discs. Within about fifteen years the hardware to read those discs had essentially vanished, and engineers had to rescue the project by emulation. The 900-year-old document outlived the 15-year-old one. "The cloud" is a lovely word for warehouses of disks with a working life of a few years, on the promise that someone, somewhere, is always copying. Someone is not always copying.

And yet our deepest problem now is the opposite of loss. We save everything—every photograph, every receipt, every idle message, every draft of every thought. An archive with no librarian. A scribe copying Aristotle onto scarce parchment was making a judgment with every line: this, not that, deserves the calf. That judgment was an act of love, and it doubled as guidance; it told each generation where to look. We have largely stopped choosing. When everything is kept, nothing is marked as important. Future historians will not lack material. They will lack a signal in it.

Borges saw the nightmare version decades ago. In "Funes the Memorious," a man falls from a horse and afterward cannot forget anything—every leaf of every tree on every day, separately and exactly. And the terrible thing is that Funes can barely think. To form the general idea "dog," you must forget the differences among all the dogs you have ever seen; thinking is subtraction. Perfect memory is perfect drowning. What saves a mind is not retention but curation, and forgetting is the curator.

Which may be why we are such unreliable rememberers. Each act of remembering seems to rewrite the memory a little; we are palimpsests ourselves, scraping and overwriting as we go, so that our oldest memories are less records than continuous retellings. That is unsettling until you consider the alternative, which is Funes.

And the honey? There is a whole small science of reading it. Under a microscope, the pollen grains in a jar name the flowers the bees visited, which names the valley, the season, the weather of one particular spring. Honey is an archive of a landscape. Somewhere there is a jar holding clover from a field that is now a parking lot; the field is gone, and its sweetness is on a shelf. Of everything we have built—marble, vellum, silicon, cloud—honey may be the most honest time capsule: no claims, no monument, just one specific spring rendered into something that keeps. Someday someone will open a jar, and a vanished field will arrive on the tongue.

Honey never spoils. Jars of it have been recovered from Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and by every account still edible—still sweet, still golden, still honey. Open it after three thousand years and nothing has degraded, nothing has been reinterpreted, nothing is a ruin. Sweetness is one of the very few things that can cross that distance intact.

Almost nothing else does. The literature of antiquity that we treat as a canon is, more honestly, a wreckage...

Sophocles wrote well over a hundred plays; seven survive. Aeschylus wrote perhaps eighty; seven. Sappho's poems once filled nine rolls of papyrus in the library of Alexandria; today we have a single complete poem and a rubble of fragments, many of which survive only because a grammarian quoted a line or two to illustrate a point of dialect. Think about that: some of the most admired poetry ever written persists in other people's footnotes. What we call the classics are less a library than the surviving debris of a library, and the survival was arbitrary. It had nothing to do with merit.

Beowulf comes down to us in one manuscript. One. It sat in a private library that caught fire in 1731; you can still see the scorch marks creeping in from the edges. The fire got the margins, not the middle, and so we have the poem—by luck, not judgment. Archimedes' most daring work, the one where he plays with infinities like a juggler, survived because a medieval monk scraped the ink off the parchment and wrote a book of prayers over it. The prayers were the reason the parchment was kept. Underneath them, faint as a watermark, the geometry waited a thousand years. It took until 1906 for someone to notice.

That's the joke of the palimpsest: destruction was the preservation. If the monk had simply thrown the old pages away, as we throw away old hard drives, the Method would be gone. Instead, by trying to erase it, he saved it.

And then there is Lucretius, whose poem On the Nature of Things argues that everything is atoms moving through void, that the gods, if they exist, are indifferent, and that there is no reason to fear death—written in the first century BC, copied and recopied through the centuries by scribes who mostly didn't believe a word of it, hanging by threads of parchment in monasteries. In 1417 a book hunter named Poggio pulled a copy off a shelf in a German monastery and carried it back to Italy, where it helped re-seed a whole civilization's imagination. How much of what we call history is the visible fraction of the near misses? Every work we still read is a survivor of fires, worms, damp walls, and ordinary indifference. For each one, imagine the hundred that got the damp wall.

That judgment was an act of love and it doubled as an act of interpretation; it told each generation what to pay attention to. We have largely stopped choosing. When everything is kept, nothing is marked as important, and the archive becomes a warehouse where significance goes to be filed. Future historians won't lack material. They'll lack a signal in it.
